# 📖 How to use this guide

This guide has one purpose: to help you **truly understand** the topics, not just memorise them.

When you understand something, you can explain it even if the professor asks the question in an unexpected way. Scripts fail. Understanding does not.

Read each section like a story. Ask yourself after every topic:

> *"Can I explain this to a friend who knows nothing about data mining — in my own words, without looking at this guide?"*

If yes → move on.
If no → re-read and try again.

**How this guide is structured:**

Every topic explains:

1. **The problem** — why does this topic exist? What were we trying to solve?
2. **The idea** — what is the solution?
3. **How it works** — the mechanism, simply explained
4. **Why it matters** — the real-world consequence
5. **A story or analogy** — something to make it stick in memory

---

# 🗺️ Part 1: The big picture — see the whole map first

Before any algorithm, you need to see **where everything fits**. This is the most important page in this guide. If you understand this map, you will never be confused about where a topic belongs.

## The one question that data mining answers

> **"What can I learn from this data?"**

There are two completely different answers to that question:

**Answer 1 — I want to PREDICT something.**
Will this customer leave? Is this email spam? Will this patient survive?
→ This is called **Supervised Learning** because the data has a "correct answer" (a target) that supervises the training.

**Answer 2 — I want to FIND PATTERNS or GROUPS.**
What types of customers do I have? Which products are bought together?
→ This is called **Unsupervised Learning** because there is no target. The algorithm finds structure on its own.

## The complete map of what you learned in Weeks 1–6

```
DATA MINING (Weeks 1–6)
│
├── SUPERVISED LEARNING — we know the answer, we want to predict it
│   │
│   ├── CLASSIFICATION — predict a category (yes/no, fraud/not fraud)
│   │   ├── Decision Trees              (Week 3)
│   │   ├── Logistic Regression         (Week 4)
│   │   ├── Naive Bayes                 (Week 5)
│   │   ├── Support Vector Machines     (Week 5)
│   │   ├── Random Forest               (Week 4–5)
│   │   ├── Gradient Boosted Machines   (Week 6)
│   │   └── Neural Networks             (Week 5 — brief)
│   │
│   └── REGRESSION — predict a number (price, salary, age)
│       └── Linear Regression           (Week 5)
│
└── UNSUPERVISED LEARNING — no target, find patterns
    └── (Covered in Week 7 — not in this guide)
```

**Practice:** close this guide and draw this map from memory on a piece of paper. If you can do that, you know the structure of the whole course.

## The workflow: CRISP-DM

Every data mining project follows the same 6 steps. Think of it as a recipe:

| Step | Question | Analogy |
|------|----------|---------|
| **1. Business Understanding** | What does the business need? | What meal do we want to cook? |
| **2. Data Understanding** | What data do we have? Is it clean? | What ingredients are in the kitchen? |
| **3. Data Preparation** | How do we organise the data? | Wash, cut, and season the ingredients |
| **4. Modeling** | What algorithm should we use? | Cook the meal |
| **5. Evaluation** | Does the model meet the business goal? | Taste the meal |
| **6. Deployment** | How do stakeholders access the results? | Serve the meal |

Two things your professor emphasised about CRISP-DM:

1. **It is iterative — not linear.** You move back and forth between phases. For example, after modeling you might discover a data problem and go back to Data Preparation.

2. **Note there are TWO data phases** before modeling — Data Understanding AND Data Preparation. Most of the real work happens before the algorithm is ever called.

# 🔑 Part 2: Three foundations — understand these or everything else is confusing

These three ideas appear in almost every question your professor could ask. If these three are solid, everything else makes more sense.

## Foundation 1: What "training a model" actually means

When we say we "train" a model, what is really happening?

Think of teaching a child to recognise cats. You show them 1,000 pictures, saying *"cat... cat... not a cat... cat..."* The child slowly learns the **pattern** of what makes something a cat — whiskers, pointy ears, tail shape. Eventually, they can look at a completely new picture and say *"cat"* — even though they have never seen that specific cat before.

A machine learning model does the same thing:

| Word | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Training data** | The 1,000 labelled pictures |
| **Training** | The process of finding the pattern |
| **Model** | The learned pattern |
| **Test data** | New pictures the model has never seen |
| **Prediction** | The model saying "cat" or "not cat" on new data |

**Why do we split into training and test sets?**

Because if you only measure accuracy on training data, the model could simply **memorise** all 1,000 pictures without learning any real pattern. It would score 100% — but fail completely on new pictures.

The test set is the honest check. It is data the model has never seen. If accuracy is still high on the test set, the model has genuinely learned something.

**The rule:** always evaluate your model on data it was NOT trained on.

---

## Foundation 2: Overfitting and Underfitting (Bias-Variance Trade-off)

This is one of the most important ideas in all of machine learning.

### The core tension

There is always a tension between a model being **too simple** and **too complex**:

- **Too simple** → misses the real pattern. Fails on both training AND test data. Called **underfitting** (high bias).
- **Too complex** → memorises random noise in the training data. Perfect on training, fails on test. Called **overfitting** (high variance).
- **Just right** → captures the real pattern, ignores noise. Good on both.

### The exam analogy (easy to remember)

| Student | What they did | Training grade | Test (real exam) grade |
|---------|--------------|----------------|------------------------|
| Lazy student | Did not study | 40% | 40% — **Underfitting** |
| Memorising student | Memorised practice test word for word | 100% | 50% — **Overfitting** |
| Smart student | Understood the concepts | 85% | 82% — **Good fit** |

The memorising student is overfitting. They will fail the real exam because it asks slightly different questions.

### How to detect it in practice

| What you see | Diagnosis |
|-------------|-----------|
| Training accuracy: 60%, Test accuracy: 60% | Underfitting |
| Training accuracy: 99%, Test accuracy: 65% | Overfitting |
| Training accuracy: 85%, Test accuracy: 82% | Good fit |

**The warning sign for overfitting:** a large gap between training and test accuracy.

### The dartboard analogy (your professor used this)

- **High bias (underfit):** darts scattered all over the board — consistently far from the bullseye
- **High variance (overfit):** darts clustered together but in the WRONG part of the board — consistent but wrong
- **Good fit:** darts clustered near the bullseye

---

## Foundation 3: Why accuracy is not enough ⭐

This one is critical. You already built this understanding yourself through our conversation, so these are your own words reflected back:

### The problem

Imagine 100 people. Only **5 are sick**. The other 95 are healthy.

A model that predicts **"healthy" for everyone** — without looking at any data at all — gets **95% accuracy**.

But it catches **zero sick people**. It is completely useless and potentially dangerous.

### Why does this happen?

Because accuracy measures **overall correctness**. It does not care whether the model is doing well on each class separately. When one class is rare (5% sick, 95% healthy), the model takes the easy path — predict the majority class always.

This is called the **imbalanced data problem**.

### What should we measure instead?

| Metric | The question it answers | Memory trick |
|--------|------------------------|--------------|
| **Recall** | Of all the people who ARE sick, how many did the model find? | **R**ecall looks at **R**eal (actual) values |
| **Precision** | Of all the people the model SAID are sick, how many actually are? | **P**recision looks at **P**redicted values |
| **F1** | A balance of both precision and recall | Use when you need both |

### When does each metric matter?

**Recall matters more** when missing a positive case is dangerous:
- Medical diagnosis — missing a sick person could cost their life
- Fraud detection — missing fraud costs money

**Precision matters more** when a false positive causes real problems:
- Spam filter — sending an important email to spam causes real harm
- Legal system — wrongly accusing an innocent person

### The precision-recall trade-off

These two metrics are in tension. If you lower the probability threshold (from 0.5 to 0.3), the model predicts "positive" more often:
- **Recall goes UP** — you catch more truly sick people
- **Precision goes DOWN** — but you also flag more healthy people as sick

You cannot maximise both at the same time. You choose which matters more for your business problem.

# 🌳 Part 3: The algorithms — understanding each one

Now we go through each algorithm. For every one, I explain **why it exists** (what problem it solves), **how it works** (simply), and **where it fits** compared to the others.

---

## Decision Trees — the simplest classifier

### Why it exists

We want a model that makes decisions by asking questions — like a doctor diagnosing a patient step by step. *"Does the patient have a fever? → Are they coughing? → Have they travelled recently?"* Each question narrows down the answer.

### How it works

A decision tree is a **flowchart of yes/no questions**. At each step, the algorithm finds the question (split) that best separates the data into pure groups.

**How does it measure "best"?** Using **entropy** or **Gini impurity** — both measure how mixed a group is.

- **Pure group** = all items belong to the same class (e.g. all survived) → entropy = 0
- **Mixed group** = items belong to different classes equally → maximum entropy

The algorithm picks the split that produces the biggest **drop in impurity** (called **information gain**). It keeps splitting until the groups are pure enough or a stopping rule is hit.

### Why it is great

- **Easy to interpret** — you can draw it and show it to anyone
- **Handles mixed data types** — numbers and categories
- **Works as an exploration tool** — tells you which features matter most
- **No need for scaling** or one-hot encoding

### Why it is not great

- **Overfits easily** — a deep tree memorises the training data
- **Not the most accurate** — other algorithms beat it
- **Unstable** — small data changes can produce very different trees
- **Greedy** — makes the locally best split at each step, not the globally best

### The key insight

One tree is like asking **one expert** for advice. They might be wrong. This is why Random Forest was invented.

---

## Random Forest — the power of many trees

### Why it exists

One decision tree is weak and unstable. What if we combined hundreds of trees and took a vote? Would that be more accurate and reliable?

**Yes.** That is exactly what Random Forest does.

### The marble jar analogy

Imagine a jar full of marbles. Ask **one person** to guess how many — they might be 30% off.

Ask **500 people** independently, take the average — you will be within 1–2% of the real number.

The wisdom of a crowd of independent guessers beats any single guesser. Random Forest uses this same principle with decision trees.

### How it creates diversity between trees

Here is the key problem: if all 500 trees see the same data, they will all produce the same tree. Voting 500 identical trees gives the same answer as one tree. Useless.

Random Forest solves this with **two types of randomness**:

**1. Bagging (row randomness)**
Each tree gets a random sample of rows, **with replacement**. This means the same row can be picked more than once. If you sample 100 rows from 100 rows with replacement, about **63% will be unique** — the rest are duplicates.

This gives each tree a slightly different dataset to learn from.

**2. Feature randomness**
At each split, only a **random subset of features** is considered (typically √number of columns). This prevents one dominant feature (like Sex in Titanic) from always being the top split in every tree.

### The result

Each tree sees different rows AND different features at each split. So each tree learns a slightly different version of the pattern. When you combine their votes:
- Individual errors cancel out
- The true signal survives
- The final model is much more accurate than any single tree

### Why it rarely overfits

Because the trees vote together. If one tree makes a mistake (overfits to some noise in its training sample), the other 499 trees outvote it.

### What you gain over a single tree

| Feature | Decision Tree | Random Forest |
|---------|---------------|---------------|
| Number of models | 1 | 500 (default) |
| Accuracy | Moderate | Usually high |
| Overfitting | Very prone | Much more resistant |
| Interpretability | High — you can draw it | Lower — but feature importance available |
| Training speed | Fast | Slower — but trees run in parallel |

---

## Gradient Boosted Machines — learning from mistakes

### Why it exists

Random Forest builds trees **independently**. What if instead, each new tree could specifically fix the errors of the previous trees? Would that be even more accurate?

**Yes.** That is the idea behind GBM.

### The guessing game analogy

Random Forest = 500 people guess the number of marbles **independently**. Take the average.

GBM = Person 1 guesses. You tell Person 2: *"They were 200 too high."* Person 2 adjusts. You tell Person 3 what's still wrong. Each person **corrects the mistakes of the previous one.**

### How it works

1. Train a small decision tree on the data
2. Look at which rows the tree got wrong — these are the **errors** (called residuals)
3. Train a **new** tree specifically on those errors
4. Add this tree to the model
5. Repeat — each new tree focuses on what the previous model still gets wrong

### The critical difference from Random Forest

| Feature | Random Forest | GBM |
|---------|---------------|-----|
| Trees built... | **independently, all at once** | **sequentially, one at a time** |
| Each tree looks at... | random sample of rows | errors of the previous model |
| Can parallelise? | **Yes** — trees are independent | **No** — each tree needs the previous one |
| Accuracy | Very good | Usually even better |
| Interpretability | Decent | Hard — each tree depends on all previous |
| Input data | Handles categories | Needs numeric input (one-hot encoding required) |

### Why GBM can be a problem

- Because trees must be built sequentially, training is **slow**
- It is powerful but can **overfit** if not tuned carefully
- It is **hard to interpret** — you cannot easily explain why it made a decision

---

## Logistic Regression — the interpretable classifier

### Why it exists

We want to predict a yes/no outcome AND understand **which features drive the prediction** and by how much. Logistic regression gives both.

### How it works

Start with the linear regression formula:
$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + ...$$

The problem: this can give any number from -∞ to +∞. We need a probability between 0 and 1.

Solution: wrap the formula in a **sigmoid function** that squashes any number into a value between 0 and 1.

- If output ≥ 0.5 → predict class 1 (e.g. survived)
- If output < 0.5 → predict class 0 (e.g. not survived)

### Why coefficients are valuable

Because the formula is additive, each coefficient tells you how much that feature pushes the prediction up or down.

**Titanic example:**
- Coefficient for Sex=male is **very negative** → being male strongly reduces survival probability
- Coefficient for Pclass is **negative** → higher class number (3rd class) reduces survival probability

This is why logistic regression is still used in business — you can explain every prediction. *"Being male reduced survival probability by this amount."*

### One-hot encoding connection

Logistic regression cannot handle text/category data directly. It needs numbers. This is where **one-hot encoding** comes in — converting "male/female" into two binary columns (1/0). R's `glm` function does this automatically.

### The probability threshold

By default, we use 0.5 as the cut-off. But you can change it:
- Lower the threshold → predict positive more often → **recall goes up, precision goes down**
- Raise the threshold → predict positive less often → **precision goes up, recall goes down**

This connects directly to Foundation 3 — you choose the threshold based on what matters for your business problem.

---

## Naive Bayes — the fast probabilistic classifier

### Why it exists

Can we use simple probability calculations to classify things quickly?

### The idea

It uses **Bayes' theorem** to ask: *"Given these features, what is the probability of each class?"*

It "flips" the question: instead of P(class | features), it calculates P(features | class) × P(class) for each class and picks the highest.

### Why it is called "naive"

It assumes all features are **completely independent** of each other given the class. This is almost never true — fever and cough are correlated when someone has flu. But the algorithm pretends they are not.

Despite this unrealistic assumption, Naive Bayes often works surprisingly well, especially for:
- **Text classification** (spam detection, sentiment analysis)
- **Small datasets** where complex models overfit
- When you need something **very fast** to train and predict

---

## Support Vector Machines — the margin maximiser

### Why it exists

When two classes are not easily separable by a straight line, can we find a smarter boundary?

### The two key ideas

**Idea 1: Maximum margin**

Don't just find any line that separates the classes. Find the line that is **as far as possible from both groups**. This gap is called the **margin**.

The data points that sit exactly on the edge of the margin are called **support vectors**. The model only cares about these points — all other points can be removed and the boundary stays the same. This makes SVM **robust to outliers**.

**Idea 2: The kernel trick**

What if the data cannot be separated by a straight line in 2D? SVM secretly maps the data into a **higher-dimensional space** where a flat boundary CAN separate the classes.

Imagine two groups of points arranged in concentric circles on a table. No straight line can separate them. But if you lift the inner circle UP into 3D, suddenly a flat surface can slice between them.

The kernel trick does this mathematically — without actually computing the higher dimensions. It just applies a mathematical function (squaring, exponential, polynomial) that has the same effect.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|------|------|
| High accuracy with little tuning | Does not scale to very large datasets |
| Robust to outliers | Must choose a kernel |
| Strong statistical basis | Harder to interpret |

---

## Neural Networks — the complex pattern finder (brief)

### Why it exists

Some patterns are too complex for any of the above algorithms — especially patterns in images, speech, and text.

### The basic idea

Layers of computational units ("neurons") pass information through the network, each layer applying a small transformation. Deep networks of many layers can learn very complex, non-linear patterns.

### Important context from your professor

> *"Neural networks are not something typically used for tabular data. For tabular data, the most powerful algorithms are SVMs, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosted Machines."*

For your Q&A, if asked: explain what neural networks are and then add that they work best on unstructured data (images, text, audio), not on tabular data like Titanic.

---

## Linear Regression — predicting numbers

### Why it exists

Sometimes we want to predict a **number**, not a category. How much will this house cost? What will this patient's blood pressure be? That is regression — predicting a continuous value.

### How it works

Fits a straight line (or a flat surface in multiple dimensions) through the data:
$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + ...$$

The coefficients (β values) are calculated to minimise the total error — specifically, the **sum of squared differences** between predicted and actual values.

### R-squared — the key evaluation metric

R² measures how much of the variation in the target the model explains.

- R² = 0 → model explains nothing, no better than guessing the average
- R² = 1 → model explains everything perfectly
- R² = 0.87 → model explains 87% of the variation

### The four assumptions

Linear regression only works well if these four conditions hold:

1. **Linearity** — the relationship between features and target is actually linear
2. **Homoscedasticity** — the spread of errors is constant across all values (no fan shape)
3. **Independence** — observations don't influence each other (time series can violate this)
4. **Normality** — the errors follow a normal distribution

If these are violated, the model may give unreliable results. Solutions include transforming variables (e.g. taking the log).

---

# 🔧 Part 4: Techniques applied with the algorithms

These are not algorithms — they are things you do **before, during, or after** training to make models work correctly.

---

## One-hot encoding — why we need it

### The problem

Most algorithms (logistic regression, SVM, GBM, neural networks) require **purely numeric input**. But real data has text: "male/female," "C/Q/S," "red/green/blue."

### The solution

Convert each category into its own **binary (0/1) column**. One column per category. Each row gets exactly one "1" — hence "one-hot."

**Before:**

| id | Embarked |
|----|----------|
| 1 | C |
| 2 | S |
| 3 | Q |

**After one-hot encoding:**

| id | Embarked_C | Embarked_S | Embarked_Q |
|----|------------|------------|------------|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

No information is lost. The data is now numeric. Algorithms can process it.

**Note:** Decision trees handle categorical data natively — they do not need this. But logistic regression, GBM, neural networks, and SVM usually do.

---

## Bagging — why sampling with replacement matters

**Bagging** = **B**ootstrap **AGG**regat**ING**

### Sampling with replacement — the key concept

Normally when you pick rows for a sample, you take a row and it is gone (sampling **without** replacement — like a lottery where each ball is removed after being drawn).

Sampling **with replacement** means: you pick a row, note it, and **put it back**. So the same row can be picked again.

If you sample 100 rows from 100 rows with replacement:
- About **63% will be unique**
- About 37% will be duplicates

### Why this matters for Random Forest

Random Forest uses bagging to give each tree a different training set. Each tree sees approximately 63% unique rows — a different 63%. This forces diversity between trees, which is what makes the ensemble work.

---

## Cross-validation — the fair evaluation method

### The problem

If you use a single 90/10 train/test split, your accuracy could be lucky or unlucky depending on which rows end up in the test set. On a small dataset like Titanic, changing the random seed can move accuracy from 73% to 81% — that is a huge range.

Which number do you trust?

### The solution — k-fold cross-validation

Instead of one split, you make **k splits** (usually 5 or 10) and train k different models:

- Round 1: train on folds 1,2,3,4 → test on fold 5
- Round 2: train on folds 1,2,3,5 → test on fold 4
- Round 3: train on folds 1,2,4,5 → test on fold 3
- Round 4: train on folds 1,3,4,5 → test on fold 2
- Round 5: train on folds 2,3,4,5 → test on fold 1

Every row is used for testing exactly once. Average the 5 test scores.

### Why this gives a better estimate

Because every row gets a turn in the test set, the result is not affected by one lucky or unlucky split. The average is **stable and reliable**.

### Important rule

Cross-validation is done on the **training data only**. You still keep a completely separate test set for the final evaluation. Cross-validation helps you pick a good model — the separate test set tells you how it truly performs.

---

## Handling imbalanced data

### The problem

When one class is rare (fraud: 0.1%, sick: 1%), most algorithms default to predicting the majority class. Accuracy looks great — but the model catches nothing useful.

### Five solutions

**1. Use better metrics**
F1, precision, recall instead of accuracy. These measure performance on the minority class.

**2. Change the probability threshold**
Lower it from 0.5 to 0.3. The model predicts "positive" more often. Recall goes up, precision goes down.

**3. Upsample the minority class**
Duplicate minority class rows until the dataset is balanced. Simple but risks overfitting to the same rows.

**4. Downsample the majority class**
Remove some majority class rows. Loses information but balances the data.

**5. SMOTE** (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique)
Instead of copying minority rows, SMOTE **creates new synthetic rows** by interpolating between existing minority examples. This adds variety without exact duplication, reducing overfitting risk.

### The key insight

When a business person says *"I need the model to find as many fraudulent transactions as possible"* — they are describing **recall**. They want the minority class found. This tells you the right metric and the right technique to use.

---

## Handling missing data

### Three options

**1. Drop the rows** — if only a few rows have missing values, simply remove them. Works when the missing data is random and few.

**2. Drop the column** — if most of the column is missing (like the Cabin field in Titanic, where ~77% are missing), the column provides little value. Remove it.

**3. Impute** — fill in a reasonable value. The most common approach: fill with the **mean** (for normally distributed data) or **median** (for skewed data).

**A smarter imputation (from Titanic):**
Instead of filling all missing ages with the overall mean (29 years), use the mean age **by gender and title**:
- Masters (young boys) get a much lower age
- Mrs (adult women) get a different age
- Mr (adult men) get yet another age

This is better because it does not force everyone to look like a middle-aged adult.

### The critical rule — avoiding leakage through imputation

**Always calculate the imputation value on the training set only.**

If you calculate the mean age on the whole dataset (training + test) and then split, the test set's values have influenced the training set. That is data leakage.

Correct order:
1. Split the data into training and test sets
2. Calculate the mean age from the **training set only**
3. Apply that mean to fill missing values in **both** training and test sets

---

## Data leakage — the accuracy that lies

### What it is

Data leakage happens when your training data contains information that **would not exist at the time of real-world prediction**. The model "cheats" — it achieves high accuracy in testing but fails completely when deployed.

### The two types

**Type 1 — Target leakage**

A predictor was recorded **after** the target event, or is a direct consequence of it.

*Titanic example:* your professor added a fake "Carpathia" field. Carpathia was the rescue ship that picked up Titanic survivors. But at the moment the Titanic sank, nobody knew which ship would save them — this information could not exist at prediction time. The model gets impossibly high accuracy. The feature is a leak.

*Medical example:* predicting if someone has cancer, but including a field showing they are taking anti-cancer medication. The medication exists **because** they have cancer — it is a consequence, not a predictor.

*Credit card example:* predicting fraud using a "card cancelled" flag. Cards are cancelled **after** fraud is discovered. The flag cannot exist at the moment you need to predict.

**Type 2 — Preparation leakage**

You use the whole dataset (including test data) to compute something like a mean, then split. The test set's information has leaked into the training process.

### How to detect it

1. **Suspiciously high accuracy** — if one feature gives near-perfect accuracy, be immediately suspicious
2. **Ask:** *"Would this feature actually exist at the moment I need to make the prediction?"*
3. **Ask:** *"Was this feature recorded before or after the target event?"*

### How to fix it

- Remove the leaking feature
- Split data **first**, compute imputation values **second** (on training set only)

---

# 🧪 Part 5: Evaluation metrics — the full picture

## For classification models

You already built the understanding of accuracy, precision, and recall. Here is the complete picture:

### The confusion matrix

For any classification model, predictions fall into four categories:

|  | **Actual: Positive** | **Actual: Negative** |
|--|---------------------|---------------------|
| **Predicted: Positive** | True Positive (TP) — correctly identified positive | False Positive (FP) — wrongly called positive |
| **Predicted: Negative** | False Negative (FN) — missed a real positive | True Negative (TN) — correctly identified negative |

**Rows = what the model predicted. Columns = what was actually true.**

### The four metrics

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$$

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad \leftarrow \text{looks at predicted positive column}$$

$$\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad \leftarrow \text{looks at actual positive column}$$

$$F1 = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

### When to use each

| Metric | Use when... | Example |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| Accuracy | Classes are balanced | Predicting iris flower type |
| Recall | Missing a positive case is costly | Medical diagnosis, fraud detection |
| Precision | A false alarm causes real harm | Spam filter, legal decisions |
| F1 | Both matter and data is imbalanced | Most real-world cases |

### ROC curve and AUC

The **ROC curve** plots True Positive Rate (recall) against False Positive Rate as you vary the probability threshold from 0 to 1.

**AUC** (Area Under the Curve) summarises the ROC curve into one number:
- AUC = 1.0 → perfect classifier
- AUC = 0.5 → no better than random guessing
- AUC = 0.81 (Titanic logistic regression result) → good classifier

A higher AUC means the model is better at separating the two classes across all possible thresholds.

## For regression models

When predicting a number, accuracy does not apply. Use these instead:

| Metric | What it measures | Notes |
|--------|-----------------|-------|
| **MAE** (Mean Absolute Error) | Average absolute difference between predicted and actual | Easy to interpret — same units as target |
| **MSE** (Mean Squared Error) | Average squared difference | Penalises large errors more than small ones |
| **RMSE** (Root Mean Squared Error) | Square root of MSE | Same units as target, like MAE but penalises large errors |
| **R²** | How much of the variance the model explains | 0 to 1, higher is better |

---

# 🔗 Part 6: How the topics connect — the big connections

One of the most impressive things you can do in a Q&A is show you see **connections between topics**. Here are the most important ones:

### Connection 1: Data leakage → missing value imputation

These two are directly linked. If you fill in missing values using the whole dataset before splitting, you commit **preparation leakage**. The fix is the same: split first, impute second.

### Connection 2: Imbalanced data → precision/recall/F1

Imbalanced data is exactly the situation where accuracy fails and you need precision, recall, or F1. These two topics always appear together.

### Connection 3: Random Forest → Bagging → Decision Trees

Random Forest is built from decision trees + bagging + feature randomness. You cannot explain Random Forest without explaining what a decision tree is and what bagging does.

### Connection 4: GBM → Random Forest

These are both ensemble methods using decision trees. The key difference: Random Forest builds trees **independently in parallel**, GBM builds trees **sequentially, each fixing the last one's errors**.

### Connection 5: Overfitting → Cross-validation

Cross-validation exists partly to detect and correct for overfitting. A model that overfits will show a big gap between its training score and its cross-validation score.

### Connection 6: Threshold → Precision/Recall trade-off → Imbalanced data

Lowering the probability threshold increases recall and decreases precision. This technique is specifically useful for imbalanced data, where you want higher recall on the minority class.

### Connection 7: One-hot encoding → Logistic regression, GBM, Neural Networks

These algorithms require numeric input. When you have categorical data (text), one-hot encoding is the bridge that makes the data usable.
